summary: Beula Edmiston, representing The Desert Protective Council, argues that the Environmental Statement is inadequate because it prioritizes ORV industry and user convenience over environmental protection. She contends that the desert is the most fragile ecosystem and cannot be rehabilitated once damaged by ORV use, and that National Parks, Monuments, and Wildlife Refuges should be closed to all recreational ORV use. She demands full and complete implementation of Executive Order 11644 without equivocation, endorsing the Sierra Club's position that ORV use should be presumed detrimental and prohibited unless proven otherwise.

It appears to The Desert Protective Council that the overriding consideration of ORV use on all Public Lands must be their impact on the human and natural environment. That "an environmental analysis will be prepared" leads to the question, by whom? The Desert Protective Council suggests that the National Environmental Protection Agency is the appropriate body and that an indepth study be made of each and every area of Public Land before it is opened to ORV use.
The Desert Protective Council endorses the proposal for full public participation in decision making.
Re ORV use on Fublic Lands, The Decert Protective Council questions the propriety of opening the door for any recreational ORV use in our National Parks, National Monuments, and National Wildlife Refuges. These areas should be closed to all but official ORV use.
The Desert Protective Council finds such statements as "such areas and trails will be selected on lands having terrain suitable to vehicle capability and having low vegetative production, erosion, and siltation potentials. Selection governed by the ability of the land and resources to withstand the various types of ORV use" far from satisfactory.
"Vehicle capability" is not the issue. The impact on the environment is. The desert, generally speaking, has "low vegetative production", yet it is the most fragile of all eco-systems, the most vulnurable to ORV use, and utterly incapable of such euphemisms as "recovery" and "rehabilitation".
It is disturbing to The Desert Protective Council that no criteria is established for determining "appropriate regulations" to assure ORV use is consistent with other activities, vegetative, and wild-life protection.

Re Alternatives, The Desert Protective Council agrees with the obvious fact that closing all Department of Interior lands to URV use would be the best alternative in terms of protecting the lands, but the sharp issue with the statement that "Closure to URV yould constitute an action inconsistent with the Department's responsibility to maintain cartain of its lands for the enjoyment and importation of the general public."
Closure to URV "ould not constitute closure to the "General Public" but rather provide equally for it on the public lands.
However, since Fundative Order 116'4 provides for controlled use of Wenth Public Lands, the Louert Protective Council will address itself to the necessity of full and complete departmental implementation of the order, without equivocation or degredation.
The Desert Protective Council questions the degree of protection in "sufficiently protected" and wonders what will constitute "significant adverse environmental impact or cause irreversible damage to existing ecological balances" and questions "rehabilitation of the land". Too often litter control is confused with rehabilitation.
REMABILITATION OF THE DESERT, THE PRIME TARGET OF ORV USE, CANNOT BE ACCUMPLISHED IN THE TIME OF MAN.
Nothing short of full and complete implementation of 11644 will do. The public, and the survival of quality, demands it.
